references.text: Earlier in the chapter, it is mentioned that it was "the first day of the week" – that is, the same day as the resurrection. The two disciples are on their way to Emmaus "on that same day" ([ref:Luk 24:1|Luke 24:1]).

After recognizing Jesus in Emmaus, the two disciples return to Jerusalem and find the eleven gathered. The journey back confirms the distance and place mentioned in verse 13 ([ref:Luk 24:33|Luke 24:33]).
Mark briefly refers to the same event where Jesus appeared "in a different form to two of them while they were walking in the countryside" ([ref:Mark 16:12|Mark 16:12]).
One of the two disciples is identified as Cleopas, which gives more information about who these "two of them" were ([ref:Luk 24:18|Luke 24:18]).

The women had already brought the message of the resurrection to "the eleven and all the rest" – this emphasizes that the two disciples were among those who had heard the news before they went to Emmaus ([ref:Luk 24:9|Luke 24:9]).

The two disciples tell Jesus about the women who were at the tomb and about some of "our group" who went there and found it just as the women had said – this confirms the context for their journey ([ref:Luk 24:22-24|Luke 24:22-24]).
Emmaus may have been identified with a village that belonged to Joshua's tribal allotment. The place name appears in some traditions linked to Joshua's land distribution ([ref:Jos 19:3|Joshua 19:3]).

The distance "sixty stadia" (about 11 km) from Jerusalem is a specific geographical indication. Similar distance indications are used in the OT to describe travel routes from Jerusalem ([ref:1 Sam 9:22|1 Samuel 9:22]).
John uses a similar distance indication with stadia to describe Bethany's distance from Jerusalem, showing that this was a common way to indicate distances in the NT ([ref:Joh 11:18|John 11:18]).
On the same day – the first day of the week – Jesus also appeared to the disciples in Jerusalem, confirming the chronological framework for the Emmaus event ([ref:Joh 20:19|John 20:19]).
